session_id.description: The session to read: the literal string "self" (default) or a sessionId from ccd_session_mgmt list_sessions.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_pr__set_monitor
tools.description: Turn this session's CI monitor switches on or off for its bound, open PR (the CI popover's checkboxes). auto_fix: the app wakes this session with a `<ci-monitor-event>` on CI failures, merge conflicts and review comments. address_comments must equal auto_fix on this machine. auto_archive_on_close: archive this session once the PR merges or closes. Pass only the switches to change, and the PR's url with auto_fix. The user is asked to approve each call (in auto mode the app may approve without asking, and in bypass permissions mode it does not ask), so only call it when the user asked for that switch.

auto_fix.description: Wake this session on CI failures, merge conflicts and review comments.

address_comments.description: Review-comment delivery. On this machine it is the same switch as auto_fix and must equal it when passed.

auto_archive_on_close.description: Archive this session once its PR merges or closes.

url.description: The bound pull request's URL, as get_status reports it. Required with auto_fix.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__start_session
tools.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so, unless it acts on what this session just found and so stays here), never what "Starting other sessions" keeps here or gives to a subagent; the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now (not for a piece "Starting other sessions" gives to a subagent). "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do, nor for the one piece of work "Starting other sessions" keeps here, nor for what it gives to a subagent. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session. Here and in `background`, put file paths and code identifiers in backticks.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), one working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one.

repository.description: With target "cloud", only when the user named a repository other than this project's: "owner/name" on github.com, which the cloud session clones at its default branch. Take the exact owner/name from the user's words or a listing that shows it; if you are not sure of it, ask them. A bypass or auto permission mode may not carry over: the session then starts in the cloud's default mode. If the call is refused, do not run or propose the other repository's work in this project.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

name.description: Server name from .claude/launch.json.

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

pattern.description: Substring filter on message text.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

lastPrompt: Add the following bench marks this compare to rust parquet and when made wasm how does it compare to js parquet libraries (chrome,Firefox, workerd)

content.thinking:
Looking at the benchmark numbers, the zig wasm reads come out fastest in every runtime, around 5 to 24ms. But zig's read only hands back column 0 as an f64 view, while the other libraries turn every column into JavaScript values. Zig does decode all columns inside wasm, so the comparison is only roughly fair.

Now I'm weighing the read comparison: zig decodes every column inside wasm but only hands back column 0 to JS, while the other libraries materialize all columns, so the advantage is partly a harness artifact and needs stating. The str_dict write in Chrome is far slower than native (423ms vs 54ms), which seems too large to be the wasm write alone. I'll time the JS-side string encoding separately from the zpb_write call at 1M rows to see where the cost actually sits.

I'm checking whether the zig adapter really does what the benchmark spec asks, and I want to see how hyparquet handles string reads, since its 511ms string-unique read is expected from decoding into JS strings. Then I'll set up the Makefile and gitignore wiring before digging into the slow zig string write.

content.text:
All three runtimes completed at 1M rows, and every reader read every writer's files at 1,000 rows. Two things need checking before these numbers are publishable:

- **String writes look anomalous.** zig-parquet's WASM string writes take 420 ms in Chrome against 54 ms natively, far more than the 2x seen for numbers.
- **The read comparison isn't equal yet.** The zig adapter hands JS only column 0, while the JS libraries materialize every column.

Wiring the make targets first, then profiling the string write in Node, which runs the same V8 engine as Chrome.

# JavaScript benchmark: zig-parquet (WASM) vs hyparquet vs parquet-wasm

Compares three Parquet libraries running inside JS engines on the six scenarios of
`zig-parquet/bench/main.zig`:

- **zig-parquet**: compiled to a freestanding `zpbench.wasm` (`make bench-wasm`).
- **hyparquet** (read) + **hyparquet-writer** (write): pure JS.
- **parquet-wasm** (arrow-rs compiled to WASM) with **apache-arrow** for tables.

Runtimes: Chrome and Firefox (Playwright drives the installed builds), and workerd (Cloudflare Workers runtime, local `workerd serve`).

## Run

From the repo root:

```sh
make bench-js-browsers ROWS=1000000   # Chrome, then Firefox
make bench-js-workerd  ROWS=1000000   # workerd
```

Or from `bench/js/` after `npm ci`:

```sh
node run-browsers.mjs 10000
node run-workerd.mjs 10000
```

`ZPBENCH_WASM` overrides the zig wasm path (default `../../zig-parquet/zig-out/bin/zpbench.wasm`).
Browser results are also written to `dist/results-browsers.json`; `FORMAT=json node run-workerd.mjs` prints workerd results as JSON.

## What is measured

- **Interop** (1000 rows, untimed): every library writes every scenario and reads every other library's output. Printed as a matrix.
- **write** = canonical JS data to a Parquet `Uint8Array`. Includes all conversion the library needs (Arrow table construction, UTF-8 encoding, copying into WASM memory, copying the result out).
- **read** = `Uint8Array` to `{rows, sum}`. Every library decodes all columns. The checksum is computed in JS over column 0 (int64 → Number, double/int32 → value, string → UTF-8 byte length, null → 0), summed in row order. A mismatch is `ERR`.
- Best of 3 runs per phase. `file_MB` is in MiB.
- Writer settings: no compression everywhere. Numerics use PLAIN encoding (no dictionary). Strings use each library's dictionary default (dictionary on, falling back to plain when it does not help).

Scenarios (see `src/gen.js`): `int64_plain`, `f64_plain`, `int64_nullable`, `str_dict`, `str_unique`, `mixed5`. Data is generated with splitmix64 (seed 42) outside the timed region.

# zig-parquet vs other Parquet libraries

Two comparisons on the six scenarios of `zig-parquet/bench/main.zig`, 1,000,000 rows,
uncompressed, numeric columns PLAIN, string columns dictionary-encoded (falling back to PLAIN
when the dictionary gets large). Each phase is the best of 3 runs; lower ms is better.

Machine: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Windows 11, 2026-11-01. Light background load (~20% CPU); treat
differences under ~10% as noise.

## Native: zig-parquet vs Rust `parquet` crate

```bash
make bench ZIG=<zig 0.16>    # zig-parquet, ReleaseFast
make bench-rust              # bench/rust: parquet 60.1.0, release + LTO, target-cpu=native
```

Both write a file, then read it back twice through two APIs. Zig's `read` is
`rowIterator()`, and Rust's `read_rows` is the `RowIter` row API: both build row objects.
Zig's `read_stream` is `rowIteratorStreaming()`, and Rust's `read_arrow` is
`ParquetRecordBatchReader`: each library's fastest reader. Zig writes numeric scenarios with
its typed column writer and string/mixed scenarios row by row with `DynamicWriter`. Rust writes
one Arrow `RecordBatch` with `ArrowWriter`.

| scenario | write Zig | write Rust | row read Zig | row read Rust | fast read Zig | fast read Rust | MB Zig / Rust |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| int64_plain | 9.1 | 8.3 | 28.3 | 88.9 | 8.9 | 2.1 | 7.63 / 7.63 |
| f64_plain | 9.6 | 7.7 | 25.3 | 89.7 | 8.0 | 2.1 | 7.63 / 7.63 |
| int64_nullable | 7.5 | 8.5 | 25.8 | 94.8 | 8.6 | 3.0 | 5.21 / 5.21 |
| str_dict | 56.8 | 18.3 | 31.1 | 159.7 | 14.8 | 4.3 | 0.84 / 0.84 |
| str_unique | 67.2 | 21.5 | 36.0 | 165.8 | 16.8 | 7.4 | 13.25 / 13.41 |
| mixed5 | 201.4 | 43.1 | 102.7 | 485.9 | 44.2 | 12.4 | 20.40 / 20.42 |

- **Numeric writes are at parity.** String and mixed writes are 3-5x slower in Zig. Zig's
  string path goes through the row-at-a-time `DynamicWriter`, and Rust writes whole columns.
- **Row-object reads: Zig is 3-5x faster** than parquet-rs's row API.
- **Fastest reads: Rust's Arrow reader is 2.3-4.2x faster** than Zig's streaming row iterator.
  Arrow decodes into columnar buffers. Zig's fastest public reader still assembles rows.
- Files are the same size within 1.2%.

## WASM: zig-parquet vs JS Parquet libraries

I've added both comparisons, run them at 1M rows, and pushed them to [Gewelf-Labs/zig-parquet#1](https://github.com/Gewelf-Labs/zig-parquet/pull/1). The write-up is [bench/COMPARE.md](bench/COMPARE.md). Every checksum passed. In all three JS runtimes, each library read every other library's files at 1,000 rows. Measurements ran one at a time on the Ryzen 9 7950X with about 20% background CPU load, so treat differences under about 10% as noise.

**Native: zig-parquet vs Rust's `parquet` crate (60.1.0)**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Numeric writes | Within 25% of each other |
| String and mixed writes | Rust is 3–5x faster |
| Row-object reads | zig-parquet is 3–5x faster than Rust's row API |
| Fastest reader each side | Rust's Arrow reader is 2.3–4.2x faster than zig-parquet's streaming iterator |
| File sizes | Same within 1.2% |

zig-parquet's two losses have the same cause. Its string writer works one row at a time and its fastest reader still assembles rows, while Rust works on whole columns. A columnar read and write API is where the next real speedup is.

**WASM: zig-parquet vs hyparquet and parquet-wasm in Chrome 156, Firefox 157 and workerd**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Reads | zig-parquet is fastest or tied everywhere: up to 31x over hyparquet and up to 5.6x over parquet-wasm |
| String and mixed writes | zig-parquet is fastest, 1.3–13x ahead; mixed5 in workerd is within 6% of parquet-wasm |
| Non-null numeric writes | parquet-wasm is 1.3–2.1x ahead of zig-parquet |
| Nullable int64 writes | zig-parquet is slightly ahead |

- **The read lead is partly API shape.** zig-parquet hands JS one column as a typed-array view, while the other two build JS values for every column. The write-up and the JS README both say this.
- **One harness fix changed the numbers.** Encoding strings one call at a time cost about 300 ms per million in browsers. Encoding them in one call cut zig-parquet's string writes in Chrome from about 420 ms to 75–96 ms. The WASM write itself runs within 1.1–2.4x of native.
- **workerd's clock was not frozen locally.** A 200 ms busy loop measured 200 ms. A deployed Worker may freeze timers during CPU work, so those numbers are local-only.

Run each comparison from the repo root:

```bash
make bench-rust
```

```bash
make bench-js-browsers
```

```bash
make bench-js-workerd
```

Firefox here is Playwright's build of version 157, not the installed copy. The new WASM bench module builds on Zig 0.16 and 0.17. CI is rerunning on the push, and Auto-fix will wake me if anything fails.

# Fuzzing and Correctness Testing Apache Parquet: Rust, C++, and the OSS Security Ecosystem ## Executive summary Apache Parquet has unusually good raw material for rigorous correctness testing: a language-neutral format specification, a substantial shared interoperability corpus, independent implementations in Rust, C++ and Java, and a mature continuous-fuzzing deployment for the C++ implementation. The strongest production fuzzing programme today is Apache Arrow C++'s Parquet integration with OSS-Fuzz. It exercises full-file reads, encoders/decoders, encryption, page indexes, Bloom filters, metadata paths and multiple batch sizes; its seed corpus combines generated valid files with both valid and intentionally bad files from `apache/parquet-testing`. OSS-Fuzz in turn runs compatible harnesses under libFuzzer, AFL++, Honggfuzz and, experimentally, Centipede, with sanitizers and distributed ClusterFuzz execution. citeturn194479search0turn194479search1 The Rust situation is materially different. The official `apache/arrow-rs` `parquet` crate is mature and actively released—`60.1.0` was published on 28 October 2026—and its test dependencies include `proptest`, `criterion`, snapshot testing and randomized test infrastructure. However, the public evidence I found does **not** show an equivalent current `arrow-rs` Parquet integration in OSS-Fuzz or a first-class `cargo-fuzz`/libFuzzer campaign comparable to C++. Instead, Rust has targeted randomized “fuzz” tests and property-based tests. A particularly revealing August 2026 issue documents a correctness bug that survived because four individually tested features—predicate pushdown, page pruning, mask-backed row selection and predicate caching—had never been tested in combination. The proposed fix is precisely the sort of cross-product, differential property testing that should become the centre of a Rust correctness programme. citeturn862759search1turn529931search0turn529931search3 The highest-value opportunity is therefore **not simply “more byte fuzzing.”** It is a layered programme combining: malformed-file coverage-guided fuzzing; schema-aware generation; property-based writer/reader round trips; metamorphic testing; independent cross-engine differential testing; systematic feature-combination generation; and regression preservation. This matters because many important Parquet failures are semantically valid enough to pass the parser yet wrong at a higher layer—for example a 2026 `arrow-rs` bug where Parquet files written with page indexes were interpreted by parquet-mr/Spark/Trino as containing zero rows. citeturn726383search43 The security record supports that conclusion. The clearest historical C++ Parquet CVE, CVE-2019-12410, involved uninitialised Arrow array memory while reading RLE null data from Parquet in Arrow 0.12.0–0.14.1. More recent OSS-Fuzz findings continue to expose undefined behaviour in C++ Parquet decoding. Adjacent ecosystem CVEs also show why differential-oracle processes must themselves be sandboxed: vulnerable historical PyArrow versions allowed arbitrary code execution when deserialising untrusted Parquet input, as did affected Arrow R releases; parquet-avro has had a schema-parsing RCE under particular Java object models. citeturn141850search0turn529931search6turn569791search0turn569791search1turn569791search2 My recommended priority order is: 1. Put `arrow-rs/parquet` into continuous OSS-Fuzz or an equivalent `cargo-fuzz` programme, with ASan/UBSan where applicable and panic/OOM/hang detection. 2. Build a **shared semantic Case generator** capable of producing schemas, Arrow values, writer properties, encodings, page layouts, compression, encryption and read-time optimisation settings. 3. Execute every generated Case against at least three independent implementation families: Arrow Rust, Arrow C++, and parquet-java; use PyArrow only as a convenient C++ frontend, **not** as an independent C++ oracle because PyArrow is based on Arrow C++. citeturn516007search10turn516007search17 4. Treat `apache/parquet-testing` as the baseline corpus, not the entire corpus: continuously add minimized fuzz failures and machine-generated boundary cases. citeturn194479search3turn194479search9 5. Add format-aware mutation that understands the footer, Thrift metadata, row groups, column chunks, page headers, indexes and encodings rather than relying predominantly on arbitrary byte mutation. 6. Measure **semantic state-space coverage** in addition to line/edge coverage: schema depth, physical/logical types, repetition levels, encodings, codecs, page versions, statistics, indexes, filters, encryption modes, null distributions, page boundaries and reader optimisation combinations. A useful way to think about the programme is: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Canonical Case generator
schema + logical rows + options] B[Valid Parquet writers] C[Structure-aware mutation] D[Raw coverage-guided mutation] E[Arrow Rust] F[Arrow C++] G[parquet-java] H[Other independent readers
DataFusion / DuckDB / Polars] I[Semantic normalizer] J{Oracles} K[Minimizer] L[Regression corpus] A --> B B --> C B --> D C --> E C --> F C --> G D --> E D --> F D --> G B --> E B --> F B --> G E --> I F --> I G --> I H --> I I --> J J -->|crash / panic / UB| K J -->|semantic mismatch| K J -->|round-trip violation| K K --> L L --> A ``` ## Implementation and resource inventory ### Core Rust and C++ libraries | Implementation | Current / relevant version | Maintainer / governance | Language | Build system | Correctness-testing relevance | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | **Apache Arrow Rust `parquet`** (`apache/arrow-rs`) | **60.1.0**, published 28 Oct 2026 | Apache Arrow project; development through GitHub issues/PRs | Rust | Cargo | Official native Rust Parquet implementation; current manifest includes `proptest`, `criterion`, `insta`, `rand`, multiple codecs, CRC and encryption features. citeturn862759search1turn529931search0turn726383search31 | | **Apache Arrow C++ Parquet** (`apache/arrow/cpp/src/parquet`) | Arrow **26.0.0**, 9 Oct 2026 | Apache Arrow PMC / contributor community | C++ | CMake, commonly Ninja | Current official C++ implementation; Parquet is integrated into Arrow C++ and has the strongest continuous fuzzing deployment. citeturn726383search1turn516007search17 | | **`parquet2`** (`jorgecarleitao/parquet2`) | Crate line 0.17.x; GitHub release 0.17.0 Nov 2022 | Jorge Carleitao / community | Rust | Cargo | Independent safe-Rust implementation; repository describes it as `unsafe`-free and integration-tested against PyArrow. Valuable as an independent historical/differential implementation, though substantially less active than `arrow-rs`. citeturn726383search9 | | **Historical `parquet-rs`** (`sunchao/parquet-rs`) | Archived 11 Jan 2021 | Sun Chao / early Rust Parquet community | Rust | Cargo | Predecessor of the Apache Rust implementation. Its weakness is that Parquet has strong structural constraints; indiscriminate mutation rapidly destroys footer and page structure, so many executions terminate near the parser entrance. OSS-Fuzz's emphasis on strong seed corpora and dictionaries is intended to alleviate exactly this problem. citeturn529931search4turn194479search0 **Structure-preserving mutation** keeps enough of the file valid to reach deep reader logic. Firebolt's open-source **FuzzBerg** is relevant here: it supports Parquet ingestion interfaces and describes its mutations as a combination of structure awareness and randomized Radamsa-based mutation, seeded through a PRNG. Its README also notes that its current model is not coverage-guided and identifies coverage-guided prioritization as future work. citeturn516007search0 For Parquet, a structure-aware mutator should know at least: ```text PAR1 header ├─ row group │ ├─ column chunk │ │ ├─ dictionary page? │ │ ├─ data page(s) │ │ ├─ bloom filter? │ │ └─ page index / offset index? │ └─ ... └─ ... Thrift FileMetaData footer length PAR1 trailer ``` **Grammar/format-aware mutation** can go further. Parquet metadata is defined through the format specification and Thrift structures; the format repository is therefore a machine-readable starting point for AST-aware metadata mutation. It should apply an ordered set of properties: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Input / generated Case] --> B{Process survives?} B -->|No| X1[Safety bug] B -->|Yes| C{Reader accepted file?} C --> D{Structural invariants hold?} D -->|No| X2[Validation bug] D --> E{Round-trip logical rows equal?} E -->|No| X3[Semantic bug] E --> F{Independent engines agree?} F -->|No| X4[Interoperability disagreement] F --> G{Optimized and reference paths agree?} G -->|No| X5[Optimization bug] G --> H[Pass] ``` For valid generated files, the strongest inexpensive oracle is usually **logical-table equality**, not encoded-byte equality. Two correct Parquet writers are free to choose different page boundaries, statistics encodings, compression streams and dictionary layouts. For one implementation, use **metamorphic** comparisons: - predicate pushdown enabled vs disabled; - page-index pruning enabled vs disabled; - row selection mask vs selector form; - sync vs async reader; - small vs large batches; - projection before vs after filtering; - dictionary vs plain writer where semantics permit; - page V1 vs V2; - statistics/Bloom filters present vs absent. This directly operationalizes the `arrow-rs` issue #10747 recommendation to compare optimized behaviour with a simpler reference configuration. citeturn529931search3 For cross-implementation testing, use at least Arrow Rust, Arrow C++, and parquet-java. PyArrow is useful as a scripting frontend but does not provide an independent C++ parser because it is based on Arrow C++. citeturn516007search10turn516007search17 Parquity's `scan` design—compare reader observations without preselecting a reference reader—is particularly sensible when the standard permits multiple representations or when one implementation may itself be wrong. citeturn726383search41 ### Minimal Rust byte harness The following is a practical starting point for `cargo-fuzz`. It is intentionally small: bytes that do not form a readable file are ordinary rejections; successful reads must not panic. ```rust #![no_main] use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target; use bytes::Bytes; use parquet::arrow::arrow_reader::ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder; fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| { // Bytes implements the random-access input abstraction used by parquet-rs. let input = Bytes::copy_from_slice(data); let Ok(builder) = ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder::try_new(input) else { return; }; let Ok(reader) = builder.with_batch_size(257).build() else { return; }; for batch in reader { match batch { Ok(batch) => { // Force materialization/use of basic structural information. let _ = batch.num_rows(); let _ = batch.num_columns(); let _ = batch.schema(); } Err(_) => return, } } }); ``` The current `parquet` crate supplies the relevant Arrow reader implementation and already has `proptest` in its dev environment; adding `cargo-fuzz` would complement, rather than replace, those semantic tests. citeturn529931search0turn529931search5 A production version should have several separate targets rather than one giant target: metadata-only parsing, page decoding, Arrow conversion, full-file reads, encrypted reads, page-index reads and writer→reader round trips. This keeps executions fast and makes coverage deficiencies diagnosable. A recommended `fuzz/Cargo.toml` skeleton is: ```toml [package] name = "parquet-fuzz" version = "0.0.0" publish = false edition = "2024" [package.metadata] cargo-fuzz = true [dependencies] libfuzzer-sys = "0.4" bytes = "1" [dependencies.parquet] path = "../parquet" features = ["arrow", "crc", "encryption"] [[bin]] name = "read_file" path = "fuzz_targets/read_file.rs" test = false doc = false bench = false ``` ### Minimal C++ libFuzzer harness This is a simplified stand-alone equivalent of the class of work performed by Arrow's own richer fuzz target: ```cpp #include #include #include #include #include #include #include extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t* data, size_t size) { auto buffer = std::make_shared(data, size); auto input = std::make_shared(buffer); std::unique_ptr reader; auto status = parquet::arrow::OpenFile(input, arrow::default_memory_pool(), &reader); if (!status.ok()) { return 0; // malformed input is expected } std::shared_ptr table; status = reader->ReadTable(&table); if (status.ok()) { // A successful parse should produce a structurally valid Arrow table. auto validation = table->ValidateFull(); if (!validation.ok()) { __builtin_trap(); } } return 0; } ``` The important design principle is the final validation step: “reader returned success” is not enough. Arrow's current fuzzing direction similarly treats structural validation as a meaningful oracle, and recent C++ bugs demonstrate that sanitizer-backed decode paths remain productive. citeturn529931search6turn862759search0 ### Schema-aware Rust property harness A higher-value semantic test generates **valid** schemas and values, writes them, and reads them through several modes. ```rust proptest! { #[test] fn parquet_roundtrip(case in arbitrary_parquet_case()) { let bytes = write_case( &case.schema, &case.rows, &case.writer_properties, )?; let reference = read_case( &bytes, ReadConfig { page_index: false, predicate_cache: false, row_selection: RowSelectionMode::Selectors, batch_size: 1024, }, )?; for config in generated_read_configs(&case) { let actual = read_case(&bytes, config)?; prop_assert_eq!( normalize(actual), normalize(reference) ); } } } ``` The critical part is `arbitrary_parquet_case()`. It should be biased toward **boundaries and feature interactions**, not uniformly random schemas. The Rust issue #10747 gives concrete high-yield dimensions: sparse single-row selections, selections crossing page boundaries, cache sizes around eviction thresholds, projections overlapping predicate columns and page sizes that interact awkwardly with batch boundaries. citeturn529931search3 ### Cross-engine harness A useful independent test protocol is: ```text Case(schema, rows, writer_options) | +--> arrow-rs writer ------+ +--> Arrow C++ writer -----+--> each .parquet file +--> parquet-java writer --+ | +-------------------+-------------------+ v v v arrow-rs reader Arrow C++ reader parquet-java reader | | | +--------- normalize logical result ---+ | compare all ``` Every failure artifact should retain: ```json { "schema": "... canonical representation ...", "logical_rows": "...", "writer": "arrow-rs", "writer_version": "60.1.0", "writer_options": { "page_version": "V2", "compression": "zstd", "dictionary": true, "page_index": true }, "readers": { "arrow-rs": "... normalized result or error ...", "arrow-cpp": "...", "parquet-java": "..." }, "input_sha256": "...", "minimized_from": "..." } ``` Parquity already embodies much of this Case-oriented philosophy and should be evaluated before inventing another outer orchestration layer. citeturn726383search41 ## CI, coverage and performance measurement ### Existing continuous-fuzzing signal The latest OSS-Fuzz Fuzz Introspector snapshot found during this research is dated 9 September 2026. It reports approximately **12.53%** project-source coverage for `parquet-arrow-fuzz` and **3.37%** for `parquet-encoding-fuzz`; the encoding fuzz target's coverage job also recorded a memory-limit problem at roughly 2.28 GB against a 2 GB limit. These percentages are Fuzz Introspector's target-level project coverage, not “12.53% of every Parquet semantic state” and not a quality score. citeturn862759search0 That distinction is important. Low aggregate source coverage can coexist with good coverage of the intended decoder, while high line coverage can still miss cross-feature combinations such as the Rust predicate-cache failure. Therefore measure both **code coverage** and **semantic coverage**. For code-level measurements, track: - functions/lines/edges reached per target; - sanitizer-specific corpus findings; - executions/second and median input size; - corpus size after minimization; - coverage delta when adding a generator or mutator; - time-to-first-hit for a fixed benchmark set. For semantic coverage, track a matrix such as: ```text Physical type × Logical type Encoding × DataPage version Compression codec × dictionary on/off Required/optional/repeated × nesting depth Null density × run-length distribution Page size × batch size Row-group size × projection width Page index × predicate type Bloom filter × predicate selectivity CRC × valid/corrupt checksum Encryption × footer/column-key mode Reader optimisation × selection representation ``` The second matrix would have exposed the exact kind of cross-product hole documented by `arrow-rs` #10747. citeturn529931search3 ### Recommended pull-request CI for Rust A reasonable GitHub Actions pattern is to use bounded fuzzing on every relevant PR and leave indefinite campaigns to OSS-Fuzz: ```yaml name: parquet-fuzz-smoke on: pull_request: paths: - "parquet/**" - "fuzz/**" jobs: fuzz: runs-on: ubuntu-latest strategy: matrix: target: - read_metadata - read_file - decode_pages - roundtrip steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: submodules: recursive - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly - run: cargo install cargo-fuzz - name: Fuzz target run: | cargo fuzz run "${{ matrix.target }}" \ corpus/"${{ matrix.target }}" \ -- -max_total_time=120 -timeout=5 - name: Replay regression corpus run: | cargo test -p parquet ``` This is a **recommended configuration**, not evidence of the current `arrow-rs` CI. The existing Rust repository does already use the shared Parquet test-data ecosystem and carries property/benchmark dependencies, while the current open issue explicitly calls for broader fuzz-state coverage. citeturn529931search0turn529931search3 ### Recommended OSS-Fuzz Rust project structure OSS-Fuzz supports Rust as a language and documents the same project model—`project.yaml`, Dockerfile and `build.sh`—used for C/C++ integrations. citeturn194479search1turn529931search4 A Rust Parquet integration should initially expose distinct targets: ```text parquet-rs-metadata-fuzz parquet-rs-page-fuzz parquet-rs-arrow-reader-fuzz parquet-rs-async-reader-fuzz parquet-rs-encryption-fuzz parquet-rs-roundtrip-fuzz parquet-rs-page-index-fuzz ``` Separating them matters because a single full-file target tends to spend most of its budget in shallow structural parsing and makes it difficult to distinguish coverage progress in codecs, page indexes, Arrow conversion and selection logic. OSS-Fuzz's own project guide strongly recommends seed corpora and supports target-specific dictionaries. For Parquet, a dictionary should include magic bytes and useful encoded tokens only where it genuinely helps; structure-aware generation is likely more valuable than a huge byte dictionary because much of the format's complexity lies in dependent length fields and Thrift metadata. citeturn529931search4 ### Benchmark methodology No comparable public benchmark was found that establishes “fuzzer A is X% better than fuzzer B for current Arrow Parquet” under controlled identical hardware and corpora. The available current quantitative source is Fuzz Introspector's target coverage, which should be treated as an operational indicator rather than a comparative research benchmark. citeturn862759search0 A proper benchmark should therefore be created. Every CI or fuzz run should report which dimensions and cross-products were observed. Populate it with historical issues from the C++ changelog, CVE-2019-12410, recent OSS-Fuzz findings and current Rust regressions. A new mutator or generator should have to demonstrate faster or more reliable discovery of those hidden known bugs before being adopted. citeturn726383search8turn141850search0turn529931search6turn529931search3 The sixth should make **regression promotion automatic**: every minimized OSS-Fuzz crash, panic or differential disagreement becomes an immutable test input plus a machine-readable description of the expected behaviour. `apache/parquet-testing` is the natural shared destination for genuinely cross-implementation fixtures; implementation-specific minimized cases can remain in each repository. The fact that the current Fuzz Introspector run itself records a memory-limit failure for the encoding target is a useful reminder that memory behaviour needs explicit measurement. citeturn862759search0 The resulting target state is stronger than conventional fuzzing: malformed bytes exercise parser safety; generated valid files exercise deep semantics; independent engines identify interoperability failures; metamorphic configurations isolate optimisation bugs; and every finding feeds a permanently growing corpus. That combination is the most likely route to finding the next class of Parquet defects that ordinary unit tests—and byte fuzzers alone—will miss.

Its README also notes that its current model is not coverage-guided and identifies coverage-guided prioritization as future work. citeturn516007search0 194 195 For Parquet, a structure-aware mutator should know at least: 196 197 ```text 198 PAR1 header 199 ├─ row group 200 │ ├─ column chunk 201 │ │ ├─ dictionary page? 202 │ │ ├─ data page(s) 203 │ │ ├─ bloom filter? 204 │ │ └─ page index / offset index? 205 │ └─ ... 206 └─ ... 207 Thrift FileMetaData 208 footer length 209 PAR1 trailer 210 ``` 211 212 **Grammar/format-aware mutation** can go further. Parquet metadata is defined through the format specification and Thrift structures; the format repository is therefore a machine-readable starting point for AST-aware metadata mutation. Page-index semantics, for example, specify relationships between `ColumnIndex`, page min/max values and scan predicates. citeturn194479search16turn194479search26 213 214 FormatFuzzer demonstrates a mature general architecture for this category: compile a binary-format template into C++ that can parse, generate and mutate valid structures, then expose a decision representation to a coverage-guided engine such as AFL. There is no evidence in the sources reviewed that Apache Parquet currently has a complete FormatFuzzer template, so building one would be new work rather than activating an existing integration. citeturn194479search14turn194479search15 215 216 **Schema-aware generation/property testing** is the most important layer for semantic correctness. Instead of mutating bytes, generate: 217 218 ```text 219 Schema 220 × row values / null pattern 221 × row-group sizing 222 × data-page sizing 223 × dictionary thresholds 224 × page V1/V2 225 × encoding 226 × compression 227 × statistics on/off 228 × page index on/off 229 × bloom filter on/off 230 × checksum on/off 231 × encryption mode 232 × Arrow schema metadata 233 × projection 234 × predicate 235 × row selection 236 × batch size 237 × async/sync reader 238 ``` 239 240 The Rust issue #10747 shows why this cross-product matters: each feature may work in isolation while a four-way interaction is wrong. citeturn529931search3 241 242 ### Fuzzer comparison 243 244 | Technique / tool | Coverage guided | Structure aware | Best use for Parquet | Current evidence | 245 |---|---:|---:|---|---| 246 | **libFuzzer** | Yes | No, unless custom mutator | Fast in-process C/C++ or Rust parser/decoder fuzzing | Used through OSS-Fuzz infrastructure. citeturn194479search1 | 247 | **AFL++** | Yes | Optional custom mutators | Alternative mutation/search heuristics; It should apply an ordered set of properties: 260 261 ```mermaid 262 flowchart TD 263 A[Input / generated Case] --> B{Process survives?} 264 B -->|No| X1[Safety bug] 265 B -->|Yes| C{Reader accepted file?} 266 C --> D{Structural invariants hold?} 267 D -->|No| X2[Validation bug] 268 D --> E{Round-trip logical rows equal?} 269 E -->|No| X3[Semantic bug] 270 E --> F{Independent engines agree?} 271 F -->|No| X4[Interoperability disagreement] 272 F --> G{Optimized and reference paths agree?} 273 G -->|No| X5[Optimization bug] 274 G --> H[Pass] 275 ``` 276 277 For valid generated files, the strongest inexpensive oracle is usually **logical-table equality**, not encoded-byte equality. Two correct Parquet writers are free to choose different page boundaries, statistics encodings, compression streams and dictionary layouts. 278 279 For one implementation, use **metamorphic** comparisons: 280 281 - predicate pushdown enabled vs disabled; 282 - page-index pruning enabled vs disabled; 283 - row selection mask vs selector form; 284 - sync vs async reader; 285 - small vs large batches; 286 - projection before vs after filtering; 287 - dictionary vs plain writer where semantics permit; 288 - page V1 vs V2; 289 - statistics/Bloom filters present vs absent. 290 291 This directly operationalizes the `arrow-rs` issue #10747 recommendation to compare optimized behaviour with a simpler reference configuration. citeturn529931search3 292 293 For cross-implementation testing, use at least Arrow Rust, Arrow C++, and parquet-java. # AGENTS.md

## Project Overview

zig-parquet is a native Parquet library written in Zig 0.16.0 and 0.17.0 (one source tree). It provides read/write support for Parquet files, a C ABI, and a CLI tool (`pqi`). Read `README.md` for the full feature list and API examples.

## Project Structure

- `zig-parquet/` - Core Parquet library
- `cli/` - `pqi` CLI tool
- `zig-{zstd,brotli,lz4,gzip,snappy}/` - Pure Zig compression codec packages
- `test-files-arrow/` - Test files generated by Python (uses uv)
- `test-files-wild/` - Real-world Parquet files for compatibility testing

### Key Files

- `zig-parquet/src/lib.zig` - Library exports (package root)
- `zig-parquet/src/core/dynamic_reader.zig` - DynamicReader (schema-agnostic row reading)
- `zig-parquet/src/core/column_decoder.zig` - Column value decoding (encodings, levels, types)
- `zig-parquet/src/core/writer.zig` - High-level typed Parquet writer
- `zig-parquet/src/core/dynamic_writer.zig` - DynamicWriter (runtime-schema row writing)
- `zig-parquet/src/core/format.zig` - Parquet format types (re-exports from format/)
- `zig-parquet/src/core/safe.zig` - Safe casting/slicing helpers for untrusted data
- `zig-parquet/src/core/arrow_batch.zig` - Arrow C Data Interface bridge
- `zig-parquet/src/core/schema.zig` - Recursive schema for nested types + logical types
- `cli/src/main.zig` - pqi CLI entry point

### Documentation

- `ROADMAP.md` - Development phases and progress
- `zig-parquet/HARDENING.md` - Hardening guidelines
- `test-files-wild/README.md` - Test file validation status

### References

- Parquet format spec: https://github.com/apache/parquet-format
- Thrift Compact Protocol: https://github.com/apache/thrift/blob/master/doc/specs/thrift-compact-protocol.md

## Build & Test

**Always run from the repo root via `make`. Never `cd` into `zig-parquet/` or `cli/`** — the tool session preserves cwd across commands, so a stray `cd` strands later commands in the wrong directory. The Makefile's recipes handle the `cd` in a subshell so the outer cwd is unchanged.

`test`, `lib`, and `cli` accept `CODECS=<spec>` and `OPT=<ReleaseSmall|ReleaseFast|ReleaseSafe|Debug>` as make variables — don't add new fixed targets for each combination.

```bash
make help                              # List all targets with examples
make build                             # Build library + CLI (defaults)
make test                              # Library tests, all codecs (Zig preferred)
make test CODECS=zig-only              # Pure Zig codecs only (no C deps)
make test CODECS=c-only                # C/C++ codecs only
make test CODECS=none                  # Non-compression tests only
make test CODECS=c-zstd,zstd           # Cross-implementation (both zstd codecs)
make lib CODECS=c-brotli OPT=ReleaseSmall  # Size-measured release build
make example NAME=basic                # Build an example (NAME is required)
make example NAME=wasm_demo OPT=ReleaseSmall
make wasm                              # Verify WASM targets compile and link
make validate-wild                     # Validate pqi against wild files (failures)
make validate-wild-all                 # Validate pqi against wild files (all)
make bench ZIG=<path> ROWS=100000      # Benchmark harness (ReleaseFast, zig-only codecs); ROWS defaults to 1000000
make bench-rust ROWS=100000            # Same scenarios with the Rust parquet crate (bench/rust)
make bench-js-browsers ROWS=100000     # zig-parquet WASM vs hyparquet / parquet-wasm in Chrome + Firefox (bench/js)
make bench-js-workerd ROWS=100000      # The same in workerd; results write-up in bench/COMPARE.md
```

### std.Io Interface

Zig 0.17 uses a unified `std.Io` interface for all I/O. File operations require an `io: std.Io` parameter.

- **In `main`**: Accept `std.process.Init` — provides `init.io`, `init.gpa`
- **In tests**: Use `std.testing.io`
- **In library code**: Thread `io` through from caller

### File I/O

```zig
// Open/create files
const file = try std.Io.Dir.cwd().openFile(io, "path.parquet", .{});
defer file.close(io);

// Positional reads (replaces seekTo + read)
const n = try file.readPositionalAll(io, buffer, offset);

// Streaming writer
var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
var file_writer = file.writerStreaming(io, &buf);
const writer: *std.Io.Writer = &file_writer.interface;
try writer.writeAll(data);
try file_writer.interface.flush();
```

### ArrayList / ArrayListUnmanaged

```zig
var list: std.ArrayList(T) = .empty;     // NOT .init(allocator), NOT .{}
try list.append(allocator, item);         // allocator passed to ALL methods
const slice = try list.toOwnedSlice(allocator);
list.deinit(allocator);
```

### Memory-backed Writers

```zig
var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(allocator);
defer out.deinit();
try out.writer.writeAll(data);
const owned = try out.toOwnedSlice();
```

### stdout / stderr

```zig
var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
const stdout = &stdout_writer.interface;
try stdout.writeAll("message\n");
try stdout_writer.interface.flush();
```

### Enum Conversion

```zig
// std.meta.intToEnum was removed — use std.enums.fromInt (returns ?T)
const codec = std.enums.fromInt(CompressionCodec, v) orelse return error.InvalidCodec;

// Use @intFromEnum / @enumFromInt (works on 0.16 and 0.17); never @backingInt / @fromBackingInt
const raw: u8 = @intFromEnum(status);
const restored: Status = @enumFromInt(raw);
```

### Target and formatting

```zig
const arch = @import("builtin").target.cpu.arch;

// std.fmt.allocPrint moved onto the allocator
const name = try std.fmt.allocPrint(allocator, "name_{d}", .{i});
```

### Custom Format Functions

```zig
pub fn format(self: @This(), writer: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
    try writer.print("{}", .{self.value});
}
```

### JSON Serialization

```zig
// Serialize
var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(allocator);
errdefer out.deinit();
try std.json.Stringify.value(data, .{}, &out.writer);
return out.toOwnedSlice();

// Parse
var parsed = try std.json.parseFromSlice(MyData, allocator, json, .{});
defer parsed.deinit();
```

```zig
_ = arena.reset(.free_all);           // NOT arena.reset()
_ = arena.reset(.retain_capacity);
```

```zig
// Zig implementations (default); C implementations opt-in via c-only or c-<codec>
pub const zig_zstd = if (build_options.enable_zig_zstd) @import("zstd.zig") else {};
pub const zig_snappy = if (build_options.enable_zig_snappy) @import("snappy.zig") else {};
pub const zstd = if (build_options.enable_zstd) @import("c_zstd.zig") else {};
pub const snappy = if (build_options.enable_snappy) @import("c_snappy.zig") else {};
```


- `export fn` does NOT use `callconv(.C)` on WASM — it won't compile.

1. Search the codebase for similar patterns first.
2. Compile incrementally — test after every 20-30 lines, not 200.
3. Read compiler errors carefully — Zig's errors are precise.
4. Never call deprecated methods — check for newer alternatives.

## Hardening Requirements

Both reader and writer handle **untrusted data**. Code must return errors instead of panicking on malformed input. See `zig-parquet/HARDENING.md` for full details.

### Never Use `@intCast` on External Data

Use `safe.zig` for all external data casting:

```zig
const safe = @import("safe.zig");

// BAD — panics if value doesn't fit
const size: usize = @intCast(header.page_size);

// GOOD — returns error if value is negative or out of range
const size = try safe.cast(header.page_size);
const count = try safe.castTo(u32, header.num_values);
```

### `catch unreachable` Requirements

When a value is mathematically guaranteed to fit, use `catch unreachable` but MUST include an inline comment explaining why:

```zig
const bit_idx: u3 = safe.castTo(u3, i % 8) catch unreachable; // i % 8 is strictly 0-7

if (value.len > std.math.maxInt(i32)) return error.ValueTooLarge;
const len = safe.castTo(i32, value.len) catch unreachable; // Checked against maxInt(i32) above
```

### Always Bounds-Check Before Slicing or Indexing

```zig
// BAD — panics if out of bounds
const value = data[offset..][0..length];

// GOOD
const value = try safe.slice(data, offset, length);
const item = try safe.get(T, data, index);
```

### Use Checked Arithmetic for External Values

```zig
// BAD — can underflow silently
const values_size = total_size - header_size;

// GOOD
if (total_size < header_size) return error.InvalidSize;
const values_size = total_size - header_size;

// GOOD
const total = std.math.add(usize, a, b) catch return error.Overflow;
```

### Return Context-Aware Errors

Use specific errors (`error.InvalidBitWidth`, `error.EndOfData`, `error.InvalidPageSize`) instead of generic `error.InvalidData`.

### Validate at API Boundaries

```zig
pub fn writeColumn(values: []const T) !void {
    if (values.len > std.math.maxInt(i32)) return error.TooManyValues;
    // ... proceed with encoding
}
```

### Common Safe Casting Helpers

- `safePageSize(i32) -> error{InvalidPageSize}!usize`
- `safeRowCount(i64) -> error{InvalidRowCount}!usize`
- `extractBitWidth([]const u8, usize) -> error{InvalidBitWidth, EndOfData}!u5`
- `safeTypeLength(?i32) -> error{InvalidTypeLength}!usize`
